title: The Bookbinder of Mainz: Arbeter Fraint, the FAUD, and Sixty Years of Exile
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Mainz, the Orphan and the Trade

stops.name: Mainz, the lithographer's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and parents from the standard biographical entry
stops.campa: A son is born in Mainz, in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, to Georg Philipp Rocker, lithographer, and Anna Margaretha Naumann. It is a Catholic working-class house in a Rhineland printing town. The father's trade is the image printed in quantity, stone to paper, and the son will spend sixty years in the neighbouring trades of the word: binding, setting type, correcting proofs, running presses in German and Yiddish and English. The father dies when the boy is four. The mother keeps the household another ten years and then dies too, in February 1887.
suggested_refs: The Rhineland printing and lithography trades of the 1870s, the family's occupation

stops.name: Mainz, the Catholic orphanage
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the month follows the mother's death in February 1887, and the day is defaulted to 01. The orphanage's exact site in Mainz is not established in reachable sources; the coordinate is a Mainz interior pin, not a located building.
stops.campa: Orphaned at fourteen, he is put into a Catholic institution in Mainz, and he does not stay in it. He runs from it more than once; on one flight he sleeps in the woods outside the city rather than go back through its doors. Nearly everything known about these months comes from his own memoirs and from nowhere else: no register, no ledger, no name of a priest or a warden survives to be set against his account. Whatever the institution means to teach him about obedience does not take. How many times he ran, and how long each flight lasted, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Rocker's memoirs, the sole source for the orphanage years

stops.name: Rotterdam, cabin boy down the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Köln-Düsseldorfer engagement is reported for roughly his fourteenth year, with no month, day, or length of service given. Month and day set to order the segment.
stops.campa: At fourteen he signs on with the Köln-Düsseldorfer steamship line as a cabin boy and rides the Rhine down through Cologne and Düsseldorf to the Dutch estuary. Rotterdam is the first place he sees that is not Mainz: a port working in five languages, dock hands and sailors and emigrant families waiting on the ships to America. Nothing in the record says how long he stayed at sea. He goes home to Mainz and takes an apprenticeship as a bookbinder and typographer. It is the journeyman's trade that will feed him in four countries, and it keeps him inside arm's reach of a press for sixty years.
suggested_refs: The Köln-Düsseldorfer Rhine steamship line, his first employer

stops.name: Mainz, the bindery and the reading circle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890; month and day defaulted. The quote is Rocker's own wording about this period, but it is preserved inside Colin Ward's introduction to The London Years rather than in Rocker's own narrative, and it is cited that way here.
stops.campa: At seventeen he joins the Social Democratic Party and starts a reading circle in Mainz that he calls Freiheit, where young workers read socialist theory aloud to one another after the shops shut. He criticises an SPD candidate in public and the party expels him for it. An organisation built to free people can also discipline them, and this one does, and he is eighteen when he learns it from the inside. He is a bookbinder with no schooling past childhood. The men he argues with about culture hold degrees.
stops.quote: It was clear to me that socialism was not a simple question of a full belly, but a question of culture that would have to enlist the sense of personality and the free initiative of the individual; without freedom it would lead only to a dismal state capitalism which would sacrifice all individual thought and feeling to a fictitious collective interest.
stops.quote_source: Rocker on his German youth, quoted in Colin Ward's Introduction to The London Years
suggested_refs: The Freiheit reading circle, Mainz, 1890
Colin Ward's Introduction to The London Years
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, Introduction by Colin Ward

stops.name: Brussels, the smuggler's pamphlets
stops.date_confidence: the congress is attested for August 1891; the day is defaulted. The detail of the smuggler Karl Höfer handing him Bakunin and Kropotkin is reported but carries no document behind it and is marked as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He goes to the International Socialist Congress in Brussels as a young dissident and comes back an anarchist. A smuggler named Karl Höfer puts pamphlets into his hands: Mikhail Bakunin, Peter Kropotkin, the argument that a workers' state is still a state and will do what states do. He reads them on the way home. In October he founds a Mainz section of the Union of Independent Socialists and begins moving anarchist literature across the Belgian and Dutch borders himself. Höfer's name comes down from Rocker's own account and from no document at all.
suggested_refs: The 1891 International Socialist Congress, Brussels
The Mainz section of the Union of Independent Socialists, founded October 1891

stops.name: Mainz, the meeting of the unemployed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of December he speaks at a meeting of the Mainz unemployed. Another speaker on the platform calls for theft; the police move on the hall, and Rocker gets clear of it by a margin the sources never measure. He is also of conscription age, so the army and the police want him for different reasons in the same month. Within days he crosses out of Germany. He is nineteen years old and a bookbinder by trade. He will not stand on German ground again until November 1918.
suggested_refs: The December 1892 unemployed workers' meeting at Mainz

segments.name: Exile: Paris and the East End

stops.name: Paris, sharing tools with Rappaport
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1893; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In Paris he falls in among the Jewish anarchist émigrés of the eastern quarters, Russians and Poles and Romanians working the sweated trades and arguing politics in Yiddish over the benches. He shares a room and his bookbinding tools with a typographer named Solomon Rappaport, who will later write The Dybbuk under the name S. Ansky. Rocker is not Jewish and cannot yet follow the arguments around him. He sits in the room while they run and understands almost none of what is being said. He is twenty years old and has been out of Germany a matter of weeks.
suggested_refs: S. Ansky (Solomon Rappaport), later author of The Dybbuk, Rocker's Paris housemate

stops.name: London, librarian of the Educational Union
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1895; month and day defaulted. The consulate visit in Paris is reported without a document and is reconstruction. The Carburton Street lodging is Rocker's own memoir detail; the memoir names only 'the Werners', so no forename is asserted here, and the street runs at roughly 51.5197, -0.1428.
stops.campa: He learns at the German consulate in Paris that going home means prison, which settles the question of exile, and he crosses to London. There he takes work as librarian of the Communist Workers' Educational Union, a German émigré club, and meets Louise Michel and Errico Malatesta across its reading room. London in 1895 holds the survivors of every failed European rising of the previous fifty years, and it holds them cheaply. His first lodging is in Carburton Street, near the Werners, a few streets off Fitzroy Square; the memoir names them only as the Werners and gives no forename.
suggested_refs: The Communist Workers' Educational Union, German émigré club, London
Carburton Street W1W, his first London address, named in The London Years
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: Whitechapel, Yiddish and Milly Witkop
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: the chronology lens dates the meeting with Milly Witkop to 1897, but Witkop's own entry states she first met Rocker in 1895, and 1897 is impossible against their joint emigration attempt of 29 May 1897. Dated 1895 here; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He moves east into the Jewish quarter and joins the Arbeter Fraint group, a gentile among Yiddish-speaking anarchists, and sets about learning the language, because he cannot organise people he cannot address. At the group's meetings he meets Milly Witkop, a Ukrainian Jewish garment worker who reached London the year before with her family. Whether the meeting falls in 1895 or in 1897 the sources do not agree; her own entry says 1895. They hold that the agreement between two people is not the state's business to register or to license. They will live together for six decades and never marry.
stops.quote: We found each other, and although each came from an entirely different world, we built a world of our own together.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, 'Milly Witkop-Rocker', memorial essay, June 1956
suggested_refs: The Arbeter Fraint group of the London East End
Rocker's 1956 memorial essay for Milly Witkop

stops.name: New York, turned back at the port
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The port of departure is nowhere stated in the reachable sources and is left blank rather than reconstructed; the refusal itself happened at New York, where the US Immigration Commissioner denied them entry.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of May they arrive at New York meaning to stay. The Immigration Commissioner asks whether they are married. They answer what is true, that they are not and do not intend to be, and they are refused entry and put back aboard the ship they came in on. The principle costs them a continent and a year. Which port they sailed from is not recorded anywhere reachable, only that they crossed the Atlantic twice inside a few weeks and landed back in England with nothing settled.
stops.quote: She opened a door in my heart which had been unknown to me before and which might never have been opened without her.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, 'Milly Witkop-Rocker', memorial essay, June 1956
suggested_refs: The London Years, chapter 6, 'Milly: How We Went to New York and Came Back'
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: Liverpool, eight issues of Dos Fraye Vort
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1897-1898; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He goes north to Liverpool, out of the East End for the first time, to edit a Yiddish weekly called Dos Fraye Vort, the Free Word, put out for the Jewish workers of the Merseyside trades. The men who set it come to the case after a full day at somebody else's bench, which is how such a paper gets made and how it usually ends. It lasts eight issues. The money runs out, as the money will run out of nearly every paper he ever edits, and the London comrades ask him back. He goes back.
suggested_refs: Dos Fraye Vort, Liverpool, 1898, eight issues

stops.name: London, editor of the Arbeter Fraint
stops.date_confidence: corrected: he first took the Arbeter Fraint editorship in October 1898, not 1899 as the chronology lens has it. Day defaulted. The Germinal dates, March 1900 to March 1903, and the Leeds year, roughly 1901-1902, are attested only to the year.
stops.campa: In October he takes over the Arbeter Fraint, the Workers' Friend, and begins publishing in Yiddish a run of essays that takes Karl Marx apart line by line: historical materialism read as a theology of the inevitable, the workers' state read as the old state with new officials in it. Nobody has argued this in Yiddish before. The paper lapses when the money does; in 1900 he founds Germinal instead, a review of literature and philosophy, and spends a year among the Jewish anarchists of Leeds while London holds together without him.
stops.quote: The Londoners looked sad and worn; they were sweatshop workers, badly paid, and half-starved.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, on the audiences at his early East End meetings
suggested_refs: Germinal, London, March 1900 to March 1903
The Leeds Jewish anarchist group, 1901-1902
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: London, the paper voted back into existence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the first issue of the new run; the conference that ordered the relaunch met 26 December 1902. The circulation figure of 5,000 is attested for early 1905, its peak, and is stated as such rather than assigned to 1903. The companion figure of 2,500 for Germinal could not be corroborated and is omitted.
stops.campa: A conference of Jewish anarchists meets in December 1902 and votes the Arbeter Fraint back into existence with Rocker as its editor. The first issue of the new run appears on the twentieth of March 1903. By early 1905 it is printing five thousand copies a week, its peak, which for a Yiddish anarchist paper in a quarter of sweatshops and lodging houses is a mass circulation. He writes most of it and corrects the rest. Three and four nights a week he is also on a platform somewhere in the East End, in front of an audience that has come straight off the machines.
stops.quote: I am an anarchist not because I believe anarchism is the final goal, but because I believe there is no such thing as a final goal.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker to the Yiddish writer Baruch Rifkin, The London Years, chapter 20
suggested_refs: The Arbeter Fraint relaunch conference, 26 December 1902
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: Whitechapel, the Great Assembly Hall after Kishinev
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1903; day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to 181-183 Mile End Road, the site of the Great Assembly Hall, roughly 500 m east of the pin the geography lens supplied.
stops.campa: News of the Kishinev pogrom reaches London in April and the East End fills the Great Assembly Hall on Mile End Road, the largest Jewish gathering the city has yet seen. Rocker speaks: a German gentile, in Yiddish, to a hall of people whose relatives have just been murdered in Bessarabia. Men in the movement had asked what a goy was doing editing their newspaper. In the course of this year they stop asking. He goes on from the hall to lecture in Leeds, in Glasgow, and in Edinburgh.
suggested_refs: The Great Assembly Hall, 181-183 Mile End Road
The Kishinev pogrom of April 1903 and its London protest meetings
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, chapter 15

stops.name: Stepney, the club on Jubilee Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Corrected: the club stood at 165 Jubilee Street in Stepney, not in Whitechapel proper; the chronology lens's coordinate sat about 1.3 km west of it.
stops.campa: On the third of February a former Methodist chapel at 165 Jubilee Street, latterly a Salvation Army depot, opens as the Workers' Friend Club. It has a hall, a library, classes, concerts, and a door open to Jewish and gentile workers alike. For four years it is the movement's actual address, the place where a man coming off a night shift can find heat, an argument, and a book he could not otherwise afford. Rocker speaks there most weeks. His son Fermin is born the following year and grows up inside it. The club closes in 1910.
suggested_refs: 165 Jubilee Street, Stepney, the Workers' Friend Club, 1906-1910

stops.name: Whitechapel, the strike that runs out of money
stops.date_confidence: attested; the strike ran 8 June to 1 July 1906
stops.campa: On the eighth of June the East End garment workers strike over wages and hours, and Rocker sits on the strike committee. It runs three weeks. He learns the arithmetic of a strike here: how many weeks of bread a community can put behind a picket line, and what occurs in the week after that. The committee counts what is in the fund each morning, and each morning there is less of it. By the first of July the money is gone. The workers go back to the machines with nothing won.
stops.quote: There was a church at the corner of Commercial Street...where at any time of the day you would see a crowd of dirty, lousy men and women, looking like scarecrows, in filthy rags, with dull hopeless faces, scratching themselves.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, on Whitechapel destitution
suggested_refs: The East End garment workers' strike, 8 June to 1 July 1906
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: Amsterdam, the International Anarchist Bureau
stops.date_confidence: attested; the congress sat 24 to 31 August 1907. Corrected: Rocker was elected one of the five members of the International Anarchist Bureau, not its secretary, as both the chronology and geography lenses had it; Alexander Schapiro is the member conventionally named as secretary.
stops.campa: He goes to Amsterdam for the International Anarchist Congress as delegate of the London Jewish federation, and argues there, alongside Errico Malatesta, for organisation against those who hold that anarchists who organise anything have already conceded the case. The question is whether the movement needs structure, and Rocker will spend thirty years answering it with unions. The congress elects a five-member International Anarchist Bureau to sit in London: Malatesta, Rocker, Alexander Schapiro, John Turner, Jean Wilquet. It does very little.
suggested_refs: The International Anarchist Congress of Amsterdam, 24-31 August 1907

stops.name: Paris, the deportation over Ferrer
stops.date_confidence: the deportation is attested to 1909 without a day; dated here shortly after Ferrer's execution of 13 October, which it answers. The stop is placed in France, where Rocker was and where he was expelled from, not at Montjuïc, where Ferrer was shot and Rocker never went.
stops.campa: Francisco Ferrer, who founded the Modern School in Barcelona, is shot by firing squad at Montjuïc Castle on the thirteenth of October. Rocker is in France. He denounces the execution in public and the French state deports him for it, back across the Channel. He has now been expelled from Germany and from France, and he is thirty-six years old, a stateless bookbinder editing a Yiddish newspaper in the East End of London. What papers, if any, he travels on after this are not stated anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The execution of Francisco Ferrer at Montjuïc Castle, Barcelona, 13 October 1909

stops.name: Whitechapel, thirteen thousand out
stops.date_confidence: attested; roughly 13,000 out, all demands met by 25 May 1912
stops.campa: Thirteen thousand East End garment workers walk out in May. Rocker chairs the finance committee, brings the Arbeter Fraint out daily for the duration, and speaks at the mass meeting on the twenty-fourth, the night on which the strike either holds or breaks. It holds. By the next morning every demand has been met. Six years earlier the same quarter went back to the machines with nothing won; this time the tailors of Whitechapel win outright, in the summer of 1912.
stops.quote: Political rights do not exist because they have been legally set down on a piece of paper, but only when they have become the ingrown habit of a people.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)
suggested_refs: The 1912 East End general tailors' strike

stops.name: London, the article of the seventh of August
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Three days after Britain enters the war he writes in the Arbeter Fraint that Europe is walking into mass murder on a scale it has never known, and that the socialist parties of the Second International, having voted the war credits in every capital that had them, have failed at the single thing they existed to prevent. He takes neither side, and there is no constituency in England for that position. He is a German who has spent nineteen years organising British workers, in a city where German has just become the enemy's language. The paper keeps printing him.
suggested_refs: Rocker's August 1914 internationalist articles in the Arbeter Fraint

stops.name: Kensington, Olympia
stops.date_confidence: arrest attested to 2 December 1914; the Olympia internment is from Rocker's own memoir, chapter 27
stops.campa: On the second of December he is arrested as an enemy alien and taken to Olympia, the West London exhibition hall converted inside a few weeks to hold thousands of German and Austrian civilians. Waiters, bakers, barbers, clerks, and a man who edits a Yiddish anarchist paper: the category is nationality and nothing else is asked. Milly Witkop is interned in her turn. The Arbeter Fraint runs on without him for a few months, and then the police close the presses and the offices both, in 1915.
suggested_refs: The London Years, chapter 27, 'Olympia'
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, chapter 27

stops.name: Off Southend, the Royal Edward
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date: the memoir devotes a chapter to the ship but the reachable excerpt gives no dates. Coordinate corrected: the Royal Edward lay off Southend-on-Sea, not at Southampton or Tilbury as the geography lens supposed, an error of roughly 190 km. The ship was sunk on 13 August 1915, which caps the period he could have been aboard.
stops.campa: From Olympia he is moved onto the Royal Edward, a converted liner anchored off Southend-on-Sea and used as a floating prison for enemy aliens. Men sleep in the holds and on the decks of a ship that is going nowhere at all. He gives a chapter of his memoirs to it, and gives it no dates, so how long he was held there cannot be said. In August the vessel is taken back into military service as a troop transport and torpedoed in the Aegean with more than nine hundred men lost. Whether he was still aboard that spring or already ashore, the memoir does not let anyone say.
suggested_refs: The London Years, chapter 28, 'The Royal Edward'
HMT Royal Edward, internment ship and troop transport, sunk 13 August 1915
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, chapter 28

stops.name: Wood Green, Alexandra Palace
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1915; month and day defaulted. Corrected: his internment there ran to March 1918, when he was exchanged out of Britain, not to 1919 as the geography lens stated. His own 'four years' is a rounding of December 1914 to March 1918 and is reported as his own account.
stops.campa: He is transferred to Alexandra Palace on its hill above north London, a pleasure palace turned first into a shelter for Belgian refugees and then into a camp for thousands of German and Austrian civilians. He is elected the prisoners' spokesman and stays it for the rest of his internment, arguing with the commandant over rations, over letters, over the men who are breaking down in the third year. By his own account he defends his fellow prisoners for four years running.
suggested_refs: The London Years, chapter 30, 'Alexandra Palace'
Alexandra Palace civilian internment camp, 1915-1919
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, chapter 30

stops.name: The Netherlands, Domela Nieuwenhuis takes him in
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1918; day defaulted. The house of Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis is not located in reachable sources, so the pin is a general Netherlands coordinate rather than an address.
stops.campa: In March a Red Cross exchange moves him out of Britain to the Netherlands, and the old Dutch socialist Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis takes him into his house. He is forty-five years old and comes out of the camps ill. Milly Witkop and their son Fermin come to him there and the family is together for the first time in three and a half years. Behind them in London the paper is closed by police, the Jubilee Street club has been gone since 1910, and the people who filled it are scattered by four years of war and internment. Where the Dutch house stood is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis, Dutch socialist, Rocker's host in 1918

segments.name: Berlin: the FAUD and the International

stops.name: Berlin, Kater's invitation
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1918; day defaulted
stops.campa: Fritz Kater writes asking him to come to Berlin and help rebuild the Free Association of German Trade Unions, and in November, with the Kaiser gone and the workers' councils sitting, he crosses into a country that had a warrant out for him when he left it. He is twenty-six years out of Germany. He arrives to find a revolution in progress and a syndicalist federation with almost nothing left of its prewar organisation. The first thing he does is sit down and write the statement of what it is for.
suggested_refs: Fritz Kater and the Free Association of German Trade Unions (FVdG), 1918

stops.name: Berlin, the FAUD founded
stops.date_confidence: attested; the twelfth FVdG congress sat 27 to 30 December 1919. The Noske imprisonment is attested to 1920 without a date and is reported here as the sequel rather than given its own stop.
stops.campa: At the twelfth congress of the FVdG, sitting in Berlin at the end of December, the federation refounds itself as the Free Workers' Union of Germany and adopts the Declaration of Syndicalist Principles that Rocker wrote for it: no parties, no dictatorship of any class over any other, direct action and the workers' own education in place of both. Gustav Landauer, murdered in Munich that May, is seven months dead, and it was Rocker who wrote his memorial essay. Within the year Noske's crackdown puts Rocker in prison, and Kater is inside with him. He finishes converting Kater to anarchism there.
stops.quote: A truly free man does not like to play the part of either the ruler or the ruled.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, Nationalism and Culture (1937), trans. Ray E. Chase
suggested_refs: The Declaration of Syndicalist Principles, adopted Berlin, December 1919
Rocker, 'Das Ende Gustav Landauers', in Gustav Landauer: Worte der Würdigung (1919)
sources: erich_muhsam.journey.json (Rocker named as author of the Landauer memorial essay)

stops.name: Berlin, the International Workers' Association
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1922; day defaulted
stops.campa: In December an international syndicalist congress meeting in Berlin founds the International Workers' Association, taking the name of Karl Marx's First International and meaning by it something the First International was not: a federation with no central authority over its sections and no party standing behind it. Rocker becomes its secretary, with Augustin Souchy and Alexander Schapiro, and writes its founding platform. For a decade the secretariat of this world organisation is a desk in Berlin. The Spanish CNT brings a million members in.
stops.quote: Organisation is, after all, only a means to an end. When it becomes an end in itself, it kills the spirit and the vital initiative of its members.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)
suggested_refs: The founding platform of the International Workers' Association (IWA-AIT), Berlin 1922

stops.name: Berlin, Makhno at the table
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and corrected: both lenses date this meeting to 1923, one of them tagging it attested. Makhno was interned in Poland through 1923, tried at Warsaw that November and moved to Torun in December; he reached Danzig only in July 1924 and left for Paris in April 1925. The Berlin meeting therefore falls between late 1924 and April 1925. Dated December 1924 as the earliest possible; treat as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Nestor Makhno reaches Berlin out of Polish internment, having fought the Whites and then the Bolsheviks across Ukraine with a peasant army and lost to both, and he comes to Rocker's rooms. Volin interprets. Ugo Fedeli is in the room. The two men share one word and very little else: one of them has commanded cavalry across a burning countryside, the other has edited newspapers in four cities and been interned in four camps. Makhno goes on to Paris in the spring of 1925.
suggested_refs: Volin and Ugo Fedeli, present at the Rocker-Makhno meeting in Berlin

stops.name: The United States, one hundred and sixty-two halls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925; month and day defaulted. The pin is New York as the tour's point of arrival; the tour itself covered the United States and Canada and cannot be given a single coordinate.
stops.campa: He crosses to North America and gives one hundred and sixty-two lectures in the immigrant halls of the United States and Canada, in German, in Yiddish, in the English he is still assembling. The audiences are garment workers, bakers, printers, cabinetmakers, the same trades as Whitechapel under different weather. On the trains between cities he begins the book that will take him twelve years, a history of the state traced back to the priesthood, which he is calling Nationalism and Culture.
suggested_refs: The 1925 North American lecture tour, 162 appearances

stops.name: Berlin, Durruti in the back room
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1928-1929 Berlin period; month and day set to order the segment. The Madrid IWA congress is attested to 1931 without a date and is reported here rather than given its own stop.
stops.campa: Buenaventura Durruti, expelled from France with police in three countries wanting him, comes to Berlin, and Rocker and Augustin Souchy hide him and keep him fed while the international secretariat goes on operating around him. Rocker is fifty-five and runs an office. Durruti is thirty-two and robs banks for the movement. In 1929 the Centre Party government expels Rocker in his turn. Two years later he is in Madrid for the IWA congress, in a Spain where the CNT has a million members.
suggested_refs: Augustin Souchy, co-host of Durruti in Berlin
The IWA congress at Madrid, 1931

stops.name: Berlin, the Reichstag burning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The Reichstag burns on the night of the twenty-seventh and the arrests begin before the smoke has cleared. Word comes that Erich Mühsam has been taken. Rocker and Milly Witkop decide that night that they are going. He is sixty years old. He has been expelled from Germany once and from France once and held in British camps for more than three years. The people around him are counselling patience. He and Witkop spend the next nine days getting out.
suggested_refs: The arrest of Erich Mühsam, February 1933

stops.name: Basel, the last unsealed train
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eighth of March they cross into Switzerland at Basel on the last train out of Germany that is not sealed and searched. He leaves behind the library, the papers, the FAUD, and the country he had come back to in 1918 to rebuild; within the year the FAUD is broken and its people are in camps or scattered. Forty-one years earlier he had gone out of Germany the first time, at nineteen, ahead of the Mainz police. He had been back fourteen years. He never sees the country again.
suggested_refs: The suppression of the FAUD, 1933

stops.name: Saint-Tropez, the book about the catastrophe
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1933, two weeks after the Basel crossing; the day is calculated from that interval rather than documented
stops.campa: Two weeks after Basel he is on the Mediterranean coast at Saint-Tropez with Emma Goldman, another anarchist without a state to be expelled from, and there he writes Der Weg ins Dritte Reich, an account of how Germany arrived where it has arrived. The study of nationalism he has been building for eight years has stopped being a study of the past; the country he left three weeks ago is now the subject. No German publisher exists for such a book any longer. It comes out in Spanish.
suggested_refs: Der Weg ins Dritte Reich, written at Saint-Tropez 1933, published in Spanish

stops.name: London, the old comrades turn out
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1933; day defaulted
stops.campa: In May he goes back to London and the East End turns out for him. The men and women who filled Jubilee Street thirty years ago are grandparents in Stepney and Whitechapel now, the Yiddish is thinner in the streets, the anarchist clubs are mostly shut, but the halls still fill for his lectures, north and east and south of the river. He is sixty years old, a refugee twice over, and holds no passport worth anything. In this quarter he has not been treated as a foreigner since 1903. He lectures across the city through the spring and the summer, and in August he sails.
stops.quote: For two whole decades I gave the best years of my life to this fine and fruitful movement. I have never regretted it. They were unforgettable years for me.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, The London Years, Author's Foreword, on the Jewish labour movement in Britain
suggested_refs: The London Years, Author's Foreword
sources: theanarchistlibrary.org, Rudolf Rocker, The London Years

stops.name: New York Harbor, the second landing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of August Rudolf Rocker and Milly Witkop land at New York and are admitted. It is the harbour that turned them back in 1897 for refusing to marry. They have not married in the thirty-six years since, and nobody this time raises the question. What was refused to a young couple holding a principle is granted to two elderly refugees from a government that would have killed them. Fermin, born in London in 1907, is waiting on the pier, and the three of them go up to Towanda in Pennsylvania, where Milly's sister has a house.
suggested_refs: The 1897 refusal at the same port, reversed

stops.name: Towanda, the memoir put down
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1934; day defaulted. The chronology and geography lenses agree on Towanda for 1933-1937 and on the interruption of the memoir by news of Mühsam's death.
stops.campa: The family lives with Milly's sister in Towanda, a small town on the Susquehanna in northern Pennsylvania. In the summer of 1934 he begins his autobiography. In July word comes that Erich Mühsam has been murdered at Oranienburg concentration camp. Rocker puts the memoir down and writes instead The Life and Suffering of Erich Mühsam, and years afterward he will write the account of Zensl Mühsam's own imprisonment as well. He comes back to the autobiography later; its second volume becomes The London Years.
suggested_refs: Rocker, Der Leidensweg von Zensl Mühsam (1949)
The murder of Erich Mühsam at Oranienburg, July 1934

stops.name: Crompond, the house at Mohegan Colony
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1937; day defaulted. Coordinate corrected: the three lenses carried three different Mohegan pins and only the geography lens's matches the settlement, at 41.309, -73.851.
stops.campa: In September they move to Mohegan Colony in Westchester County, some fifty miles up from New York City: a settlement grown around a libertarian school, houses among the trees, a few hundred people who came out of much the same immigrant radical world he did. He is sixty-four. He has lived in Mainz, Rotterdam, Paris, London, Liverpool, Leeds, Berlin, Towanda, and four British internment camps. This is the last address. He keeps it for twenty-one years.
suggested_refs: Mohegan Colony, Westchester County, New York, and its libertarian school

stops.name: Mohegan Colony, Nationalism and Culture
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1937; month and day set to follow the September move. The chronology lens's claim that a Spanish edition appeared 'the same year' in Barcelona is not supported: the source gives a three-volume Barcelona edition with no year, and the clause is dropped here.
stops.campa: Nationalism and Culture is published, twelve years after he started it on American trains. It argues that the state descends from the priesthood and not from any social contract; that every political theology from the divine right of kings to the dictatorship of the proletariat is the same claim in different clothing; and that culture and political power grow in inverse proportion to one another. Thomas Mann and Bertrand Russell read it and say so in print. A Spanish edition appears in three volumes in Barcelona.
stops.quote: The deeper we trace the political influences in history, the more are we convinced that the 'will to power' has up to now been one of the strongest motives in the development of human social forms.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, Nationalism and Culture (1937), trans. Ray E. Chase
suggested_refs: Nationalism and Culture, trans. Ray E. Chase, 1937
The three-volume Barcelona edition, year not established

stops.name: Mohegan Colony, Anarcho-Syndicalism
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1938, first issued in Britain; month and day defaulted. Chomsky's 1970 introduction is cited as reception of the book, not as an event in Rocker's own life.
stops.campa: He writes Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice, and it becomes the book his name carries. The argument is short and old: the union is at once the weapon that breaks the present order and the cell of the order meant to replace it, so the thing that fights must already be shaped like the thing that comes after. He has been writing on Spain for two years, where the CNT collectives are proving the case and losing the war in the same months. The book has never gone out of print. Noam Chomsky introduced the 1970 edition.
stops.quote: Freedom is the very essence of life, the impelling force in all intellectual and social development.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Rocker, Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938), opening chapter
suggested_refs: Rocker, The Truth About Spain (1936), and his articles in The Spanish Revolution
Noam Chomsky's 1970 introduction to Anarcho-Syndicalism

stops.name: Mohegan Colony, the parcels to Germany
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1946; day defaulted
stops.campa: An appeal in the Freie Arbeiter Stimme sets out what is left of the German anarchists after twelve years: survivors of camps and prisons in a country with no food in it. From Mohegan, Rocker organises a parcel operation and keeps it running, food and clothing crossing the Atlantic to men and women he last saw in Berlin in 1933. He is seventy-three years old. Three years later he publishes Pioneers of American Freedom, a history of liberal and anarchist thought in the United States.
suggested_refs: The Freie Arbeiter Stimme appeal of 1946
Rocker, Pioneers of American Freedom (1949)

stops.name: Mohegan Colony, the eightieth birthday
stops.date_confidence: the dinner and the tributes are attested to 1953; the date is his birthday, and whether the dinner fell on it is not stated. The stop is placed at Mohegan, not in London: he gave up the lecture circuit after an operation in 1939 and no source says he attended.
stops.campa: A dinner is held for his eightieth birthday in London, and tributes are read out from Thomas Mann, Albert Einstein, Herbert Read, and Bertrand Russell. The bookbinder who left school as a child, was thrown out of the Social Democratic Party at eighteen and out of Germany at nineteen, is saluted by the literary and scientific establishment of two continents, in the city where he once edited a Yiddish weekly for men working eighteen hours a day. He is at Mohegan. He gave up travelling in 1939, after an operation, and no account says he was there.
suggested_refs: The London eightieth-birthday dinner, 1953, and its written tributes

stops.name: Mohegan Colony, the record stops
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both the English and German entries, which agree on the place as Mohegan Colony near Crompond and the age as 85. Open gap: no cemetery, marker, or disposition of the remains could be confirmed; the Find a Grave search interface blocked automated access.
stops.campa: Milly Witkop dies before him; his memorial essay for her appears in June 1956, sixty-one years after they met at an Arbeter Fraint meeting in Whitechapel. Rudolf Rocker dies at Mohegan Colony on the nineteenth of September 1958, aged eighty-five. Where he is buried is not recorded in anything reachable: no cemetery named, no marker described, no account of what was done with the remains. The English entry gives the death and stops. So does the German. No death date for Milly Witkop is recorded either.
suggested_refs: Rocker, 'Milly Witkop-Rocker', memorial essay, June 1956

stops.name: Amsterdam, the papers on the Cruquiusweg
stops.date_confidence: the archive holding is attested; the date of deposit is not, and the date given here is the year the institute moved to Cruquiusweg 31, where the papers now sit. Coordinate corrected: the geography supplied by the afterlife lens was about 2.2 km off, in the Rivierenbuurt.
stops.campa: His papers, letters, and manuscripts are held at the International Institute of Social History on the Cruquiusweg in Amsterdam-Oost: the correspondence of the Arbeter Fraint years, of the FAUD, of the IWA secretariat, four decades of a movement that kept almost nothing else. A microfilm copy sits at the German National Library in Leipzig, so that the country which expelled him twice can read him at home. He never in his life held an office any state recognised. When the papers were deposited is not recorded; the institute moved to this address in 1989.
suggested_refs: The Rudolf Rocker Papers, International Institute of Social History, Cruquiusweg 31, Amsterdam
The Leipzig microfilm copy, Deutsche Nationalbibliothek, Deutscher Platz 1
sources: Dutch Wikipedia, 'Internationaal Instituut voor Sociale Geschiedenis'

stops.name: Mainz, the institute in the birthplace
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 2024 on the German entry only; the institute's own website was unreachable and no further detail could be verified. Day defaulted.
stops.campa: A Rudolf-Rocker-Institut opens in Mainz in June 2024, a research centre for his life and his work, in the city where he was born, orphaned, apprenticed, expelled from a political party, and very nearly taken off a platform by police. It is a hundred and fifty-one years after his birth and sixty-six years after his death. He left Mainz at nineteen with the police behind him and never lived in it again; he wrote in German for the rest of his life, and was published in it hardly at all between 1933 and the year he died. German editions of the memoirs began appearing in 1974.
suggested_refs: The Rudolf-Rocker-Institut, Mainz, founded June 2024

stops.name: Berlin-Britz, two stones at Buschkrugallee 246
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 2024 on the German entry; day defaulted. The Buschkrugallee address as a Rocker residence rests on that entry alone and is not corroborated elsewhere in the material gathered.
stops.campa: Two brass stones are set into the pavement outside Buschkrugallee 246 in Berlin-Britz, where Rudolf Rocker and Milly Witkop lived before 1933. Stolpersteine, the small square plaques laid across Europe for people driven out or killed, name them both. They go in ninety-one years after the couple crossed at Basel on an unsealed train. Neither of the two died in a camp; both got out, which is not the usual reason for a stone. That the address was theirs rests on a single German source and is corroborated nowhere else.
suggested_refs: The Stolpersteine for Rudolf Rocker and Milly Witkop, Buschkrugallee 246, Berlin-Britz, July 2024
